prompt: A system's database spends most of its time answering reads of the same rows. Which technique answers that problem first?

choices.text: Sharding by the most-read column, so that each server answers part of the reads
choices.why: Sharding splits writes and size, at a permanent cost to every query; reads are cheaper to solve with replicas.

choices.text: Replication
choices.why: Right. Replicas take reads; every copy holds everything.

choices.text: Partitioning the table by month
choices.why: Partitioning makes queries on a range cheaper; it does not add a server to answer them.

choices.text: A bigger index on the read column
choices.why: The rows are already found; the problem is how many times they are asked for.

prompt: Why does the lesson reach for sharding last?

choices.text: PostgreSQL does not support it
choices.why: The lab ran it on two PostgreSQL servers; the routing lives in the program.

choices.text: It only helps reads, which replicas already handle
choices.why: Sharding is what scales writes; that is its reason to exist.

choices.text: It changes every query the program makes, for good
choices.why: Right. Each query has to choose a shard or ask them all, and that is hard to undo.

choices.text: It needs a different database for each shard, from a different vendor, so that a bug in one does not reach the others
choices.why: The shards in the lab are the same PostgreSQL image.

prompt: What does a PostgreSQL replica receive from the primary, in streaming replication?

choices.text: Each SQL statement a client sent, to run again on the replica's own copy of the data
choices.why: It receives the changes the statements made, not the statements; a statement with now() would give a different result twice.

choices.text: A full copy of the data every few minutes
choices.why: A full copy happens once, with pg_basebackup; afterwards only the log flows.

choices.text: Only the rows clients have read recently
choices.why: That would be a cache; a replica holds everything.

choices.text: The write-ahead log, as it is written
choices.why: Right. The replica applies the same changes in the same order.

prompt: pg_stat_replication shows sync_state = async. What does that mean for a client whose INSERT just returned?

choices.text: The replica may not have the row yet
choices.why: Right. The primary did not wait for the replica before answering.

choices.text: The replica received the row and will apply it at night
choices.why: It applies changes continuously, a moment behind.

choices.text: The row exists on both servers already
choices.why: That is the guarantee synchronous replication gives, in lesson 3.

choices.text: The INSERT was queued and may still fail
choices.why: It committed on the primary; only the replica's copy is late.

prompt: Why does a replica refuse an UPDATE?

choices.text: Two servers accepting writes to the same rows would have to agree on the result
choices.why: Right. A replica avoids the problem by never writing.

choices.text: Its disk is mounted read-only
choices.why: It writes to its disk all the time, applying the log.

choices.text: Replicas run an older version of PostgreSQL
choices.why: Both containers run postgres:16.15.

choices.text: The replicator user has no write permission
choices.why: The UPDATE ran as the tickets user, which can write on the primary; the refusal is about being a replica.

prompt: The command that copies the primary's whole data directory to start a replica is pg____ .
Which read should go to the primary rather than a replica?

choices.text: Checking that a seat is free just before selling it
choices.why: Right. A read that decides a write must see the latest state.

choices.text: The list of venues
choices.why: It changes rarely; a replica's copy is fine.

choices.text: The page of a show browsed by a visitor
choices.why: The bulk of the traffic, and a second's staleness hurts nobody.

choices.text: A dashboard of sales per day, refreshed every minute
choices.why: Nobody can tell a figure a second old; it is a natural replica read.

prompt: A system's problem is too many writes. Why do more replicas not help?

choices.text: Every replica repeats every write
choices.why: Right. Replicas add read capacity; the write work is applied everywhere.

choices.text: Replicas slow the primary's writes by locking its rows while they copy them
choices.why: Replicas read the log; they take no locks on the primary's rows.

choices.text: PostgreSQL limits a primary to one replica
choices.why: max_wal_senders allows ten by default.

choices.text: Writes have to be sent to every replica by the program
choices.why: The program writes once to the primary; replication does the rest.

prompt: After five seconds of reads, the replica's xact_commit went from 3 to 8027 while load.py sent 9655 requests. What explains the difference?

choices.text: nginx answered 1600 from its cache
choices.why: This nginx caches nothing.

choices.text: 1600 requests failed
choices.why: The status line showed 9655 answers of 200.

choices.text: The counter is updated in batches, so it trails the requests
choices.why: Right. The reads did reach the replica.

choices.text: About 1600 reads went to the primary instead
choices.why: Every GET in app.py asks db(REPLICA).

prompt: A buyer buys a ticket and the next page says it was never sold. Which guarantee was lost?

choices.text: Isolation between two buyers of the same show
choices.why: One buyer, reading their own write.

choices.text: Read-your-writes
choices.why: Right. The read came from a replica that had not applied the sale.

choices.text: Atomicity, because the sale was applied in two halves
choices.why: The sale committed whole; the replica had not applied any of it.

choices.text: Durability
choices.why: The sale is safe on the primary; it is only not visible yet.

prompt: A program stores the primary's pg_current_wal_lsn() after each of a user's writes. What does it do with it before reading from a replica?

choices.text: Sends the LSN to the replica so that it applies the log up to that point immediately
choices.why: A replica applies the log as fast as it can already; the program can only wait or go elsewhere.

choices.text: Compares it with the time of the read
choices.why: An LSN is a position in the log, not a time.

choices.text: Uses it as the id of the ticket
choices.why: It identifies a place in the log, not a row.

choices.text: Checks the replica's pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() is at least that
choices.why: Right. If it is, the replica has applied the user's write.

prompt: What is the weakness of 'read from the primary for a few seconds after each write'?

choices.text: It sends every read in the system to the primary
choices.why: Only the reads of users who just wrote.

choices.text: The few seconds are a guess about the worst lag
choices.why: Right. A replica further behind than the guess still serves a stale read.

choices.text: It needs synchronous replication
choices.why: It works with asynchronous replicas; that is its point.

choices.text: It cannot be implemented without changing PostgreSQL
choices.why: It is a decision in the program: a timestamp in the session.

prompt: Put the events of an asynchronous write in order, as the replica's reader experiences them.
items: The primary writes the change to its WAL
The client is told the transaction committed
The replica receives the log record
The replica applies it, and reads there see the change

prompt: With the primary stopped, the box office's sales fail and its show pages still load. Why?

choices.text: The replica promoted itself when the primary stopped
choices.why: It was promoted by hand afterwards; until then it stayed read-only.

choices.text: nginx serves the pages from a copy it kept in memory before the primary stopped
choices.why: This nginx keeps no copies; every page came from the replica.

choices.text: Pages are read from the replica, which is still up
choices.why: Right. Sales need the primary; reads were routed elsewhere.

choices.text: The app retries sales until they work
choices.why: The sale returned a 502 at once.

prompt: After promoting an asynchronous replica, which sales can be lost?

choices.text: All sales of the last hour, because replicas copy hourly
choices.why: Replicas follow continuously; the loss is the lag at the moment of failure.

choices.text: Only sales in progress, which the client never saw confirmed
choices.why: Those are lost too, but the dangerous ones are the confirmed ones.

choices.text: Those committed on the old primary but not yet sent
choices.why: Right. They exist only on the dead machine.

choices.text: None; a promoted replica fetches the missing log from the dead primary when it starts
choices.why: The primary is dead; there is nothing to fetch from.

prompt: Match each failover hazard to what defends against it.

pairs.left: the program still points at the old primary
pairs.right: a proxy or a name that moves to the new one

pairs.left: confirmed writes lost with the old machine
the old primary returns and accepts writes

prompt: The plan for a June query on the partitioned sales table reads sales_2026_06 only. What is that called?

choices.text: Replication lag
choices.why: Nothing in this query involves a replica.

choices.text: An index-only scan of the parent table, which stores a summary of every child
choices.why: The parent holds no rows; the plan scans one child.

choices.text: Partition pruning
choices.why: Right. The planner ruled out five partitions from the filter.

choices.text: Sharding by month
choices.why: All six partitions are on one server.

prompt: On the sales table of the lesson, a sale dated 2026-07-03 is inserted. What happens?

choices.text: It is stored in the parent table
choices.why: A partitioned parent holds no rows of its own.

choices.text: The insert fails: no partition holds July
choices.why: Right. Someone has to create July's partition first.

choices.text: It goes into June's partition, the last one
choices.why: A range partition only takes rows inside its range.

choices.text: PostgreSQL creates a July partition automatically
choices.why: It does not; that is why a scheduled job exists.

prompt: On a sales table partitioned by month, a report asks for every sale of show 42 since the table began. How does partitioning affect it?

choices.text: Six times faster, because the partitions are read in parallel
choices.why: Parallel reads of six pieces do the same work as one table, plus six plans.

choices.text: Slightly slower: every partition is read
choices.why: Right. Pruning needs a filter on the key; show 42 is not the key.

choices.text: It fails, because the query does not name a month
choices.why: Queries on the parent work with any filter; only pruning needs the key.

choices.text: It reads only the most recent partition
choices.why: That would miss earlier sales; the planner cannot rule any out.

prompt: Apart from time, what does a big DELETE cost that dropping a partition does not?

choices.text: It cannot be rolled back
choices.why: The lesson's DELETE was rolled back.

choices.text: It needs the table to be detached first
choices.why: A DELETE works on the parent directly.

choices.text: Every row's removal goes into the log and to every replica
choices.why: Right, and the dead rows stay on disk until VACUUM.

choices.text: It deletes rows from other partitions as well
choices.why: Its WHERE limits it to January.

prompt: In the capture, how many rows did the DELETE remove from January?
The box office is sharded by show. Which operation touches exactly one shard?

choices.text: Listing the ten best-selling shows of the week
choices.why: Every shard holds some shows; all must be asked.

choices.text: Selling a ticket for show 42
choices.why: Right. The show's row and its tickets live on one shard.

choices.text: Counting all tickets sold
choices.why: Each shard counts its own; the program adds.

choices.text: Finding every ticket one buyer has bought, across all the shows they went to this year
choices.why: A buyer's tickets are spread over the shards of their shows.

prompt: Sharding by show, one concert takes 80% of all sales. What happens?

choices.text: The router spreads that show over every shard
choices.why: shard_for gives one answer per show.

choices.text: Nothing; the sales are divided evenly by hashing
choices.why: The hash divides shows, not sales of one show.

choices.text: Its shard is overloaded while the others idle
choices.why: Right. A hot key cannot be split by sharding on that key.

choices.text: Adding a shard solves it
choices.why: The hot show still lands on one shard.

prompt: With the lesson's router and two shards, show n sells n tickets for n = 1 to 100. How many tickets end up on shard 0?
Each shard returns the average ticket price of its own shows. Why is the average of those averages wrong?

choices.text: The shards hold different numbers of tickets
choices.why: Right. Each shard should return a sum and a count, which do merge.

choices.text: One shard's answer always arrives late
choices.why: Late or not, the arithmetic is wrong.

choices.text: Prices are stored in cents, so dividing by the number of shards rounds every average down
choices.why: Rounding is not the issue; the weights are.

choices.text: Averages cannot be computed in SQL
choices.why: avg() exists; merging them is the problem.

prompt: Two shards each create rows in a table with a bigserial id. What goes wrong?

choices.text: Both hand out the same ids
choices.why: Right. Each shard has its own sequence.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as each shard has its own primary key
choices.why: Each key is unique only inside its shard.

choices.text: The ids skip every other number because the two sequences take turns
choices.why: The sequences know nothing of each other.

choices.text: Inserts fail on the second shard
choices.why: Each shard's insert succeeds; the clash is between shards.

prompt: Why is the shard key chosen so that common operations stay inside one shard?

choices.text: Routers can only reach one shard per connection, so a second shard means opening a new connection each time
choices.why: The router keeps a connection to every shard.

choices.text: Locks are not available across shards
choices.why: Locks exist on each shard; atomicity across them does not.

choices.text: No ordinary transaction spans two servers
choices.why: Right. Two-phase commit and sagas exist, and both are expensive.

choices.text: Shards cannot read each other's tables
choices.why: True, and not the reason; the program reads both.

prompt: By modulo, about what share of keys move when going from 4 shards to 5?

choices.text: One fifth
choices.why: That is the minimum, which the ring approaches.

choices.text: Four fifths
choices.why: Right. n / (n + 1), with n = 4.

choices.text: None, because the old shards keep their keys
choices.why: The remainder of almost every key changes.

choices.text: A quarter
choices.why: Each old shard gives a quarter only under a ring.

prompt: With 10 points per shard, the ring moved only 26.2% of keys. Why is that not a better result than 1000 points?

choices.text: 26.2% is below the minimum, so it is a measurement error
choices.why: The minimum applies to an even split; this split was not even.

choices.text: Fewer points make lookups slower
choices.why: Fewer points make lookups faster.

choices.text: It is better; fewer keys moving is always the goal
choices.why: Moving fewer keys by leaving a shard underused is not a saving.

choices.text: The shards ended very uneven, one with almost twice another's keys
choices.why: Right. Fewer moves came from the new shard getting less than its share.

prompt: What does creating 256 logical shards on four servers from the start buy?

choices.text: A key's logical shard never changes; only the map to servers does
choices.why: Right. Whole logical shards move, and no key is re-hashed.

choices.text: Cross-shard transactions become ordinary ones, because logical shards share a server
choices.why: Two logical shards may sit on different servers at any time.

choices.text: No need for a shard key
choices.why: The key still picks the logical shard.

choices.text: 256 times the write capacity
choices.why: Capacity is still four servers' worth.

prompt: Match each problem to the technique the lesson uses for it.

pairs.left: too many writes for one server
surviving the loss of the primary

prompt: A ticketing system shards by buyer. What becomes a cross-shard operation that sharding by show would have kept local?

choices.text: Inserting a ticket
choices.why: An insert lands on the buyer's shard.

choices.text: Reading a buyer's profile
choices.why: Local to the buyer's shard.

choices.text: Showing one buyer their own tickets
choices.why: That becomes local when the buyer is the key.

choices.text: Selling the last seats of one show
choices.why: Right. Buyers of one show are on many shards, and the seat count must be checked against all of them.

prompt: A query with no shard key is sent to every shard and the answers merged; this is called scatter-___ .
